quotes.verbatim_quote:
The key changes from C to D moving chromatically by half step. Don’t let the chord quality get in
the way of your analysis. It can be simple or sophisticated.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Teaches chromatic half-step modulation, emphasizing that chord quality and root position are flexible.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Approaching a chord from a half step above or belowis another accepted way of moving the harmony.
The A13 in measure two — the V7 of the new key of D — is approached by Bb13 in the first measure. The
inner descending line in measure two is interesting enough to stay where itis for four beats before moving
quotes.why_load_bearing: Names half-step chord approach as a standard harmonic movement technique, with the V7 of the new key approached from a half step above.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
A major scale can within itself provide cyclical movement, although not with
exact perfect fifth intervals throughout. This within-the-scale cycle is used here
through the Dm7, after which a’ VI (A’6) of the C scale is inserted. This deceptive
cadence opens up several possibilities, but since we want to move on to E>, we'll
stay with the A’6 as the way to go.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Describes how the major scale provides an approximate cycle of fifths internally and demonstrates the deceptive cadence as a modulation pivot.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Ultimately, whatever sounds good to the ear will probably work. Just go there. Of course, if all
your playing buddies grimace, you do have to remember that there are community standards of
decency.
quotes.why_load_bearing: States that ear-based judgment ultimately governs harmonic choices, balanced by ensemble taste.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Since being taught to death is a horrible way to die, I've decided to make Part 7 a group of tunes
without analysis, explanation or instruction. Just a personal word or two. Do | hear cheering?

| call these pieces Fun Jazz, as they were fun for me to create. | didn’t sit down and compose
them. They are improvisations based on standard chord changes which you may recognize.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Frames Part 7 as unanalyzed improvisations over standard changes, shifting from instruction to creative example.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
In all of the tunes here | like to imply more with less. Chords, for instance, are most often only
two or three notes, and the melody is all-important.
quotes.why_load_bearing: States the core fingerstyle principle of implying harmony with minimal chord voicings (two or three notes) while prioritizing melody.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
In the days of Vaudeville, musicians used to play a purposely silly ending called "good evening friends." I decided to make the four-note theme into a blues.
There are three independent voices at once in this piece, if you count a whole note as a voice. It is. Play the piece with an underlying triplet feel.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Describes treating three independent voices simultaneously and applying a triplet feel to the piece.

quotes.verbatim_quote: This Fats Waller imitation starts with a solid stride style. After a while I sneak bebop into it. Ragtime bebop? Why not?
quotes.why_load_bearing: Demonstrates blending stride piano style with bebop on guitar, crossing genre boundaries.

quotes.verbatim_quote: I love ballads. They allow a player to have as much elbow room to do whatever he wants, such as playing in double time feel.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Names ballads as the form giving maximum freedom, including double-time feel shifts.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
This blues is sparse in bass notes yet feels as though nothing is missing. One way this is accom-
plished is by using an almost continual eighth note flow. Joe Pass often used this device.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Credits Joe Pass for the continual eighth-note flow technique that compensates for sparse bass notes in blues.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
This improvisation was included in an earlier book of mine, Jazz in Position (Mel Bay
Publications, Inc.). That was a book for pick guitar, and the melodic line was just one note with
no accompaniment. Here | fleshed it out and turned it into a self-accompanied fingerstyle
arrangement. You can do this with virtually any existing tune you have been playing as a single
line only. The chord structure is similar to Lullaby of Birdland.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Teaches the technique of converting any single-line melody into a self-accompanied fingerstyle arrangement.

quotes.verbatim_quote: 3 on 4 takes its name from having many three-beat phrases in the context of 4/4 measures. The melodic line is primarily accompanied by tri-tones. This is the type of sparse playing that could easily fit in a trio or quartet setting.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Names the three-over-four polyrhythmic device accompanied by tritones as sparse playing suitable for ensemble contexts.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
A walkdown is a descending bass line with a common tone on top of a chord stack. This is the

device that keeps popping up in this tune along with its hook-like rhythm.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines the walkdown as a descending bass line under a common-tone chord stack, a recurring compositional device.
